structure.title: PART I
structure.heading: PART I
structure.start_phrase:
We
 started Square in February 2009 to enable businesses (sellers) to accept card payments, an important capability that was previously inaccessible to many
 businesses.
structure.summary:
- Overview and mission: Square, founded in February 2009, aims to economically empower businesses by giving them accessible, affordable tools to accept payments and run their operations within a cohesive commerce ecosystem.
- Differentiation and design: Combines sophisticated software with affordable hardware to turn mobile/computing devices into POS systems; emphasizes fast, self-serve, dependable products and robust risk management using data science and machine learning, achieving high seller acceptance with low fraud losses.
- Core payments platform: Full-service managed payments with rapid onboarding; accepts in-person magstripe (swipe), EMV (dip), NFC (tap), and online via Square Invoices, Virtual Terminal, and merchant websites; provides reporting/analytics, next-day settlements, digital receipts, dispute management/chargeback protection, and PCI compliance.
- Consumer side: Square Cash enables individuals to send and receive money with people and businesses.
- Point-of-sale software and services: Tools for analytics and reporting; order, inventory, location, employee, and payroll management; customer engagement features; monetized via per-transaction, subscription, or service fees.
- Financial services: Square Capital facilitates business loans based on sellers’ processing histories.
- Platform and vertical solutions: Build with Square APIs for customized solutions and third-party integrations; vertical-specific tools such as Invoices, Appointments, and Inventory; Caviar food ordering service helps restaurants reach new customers.
- Scale and markets: Serves millions of sellers across retail, services, and food sectors, from sole proprietors to multi-location businesses in the U.S., Canada, Japan, and Australia.
- Volume and growth metrics: Processed $49.7B GPV in 2016 (1B card payments from ~245M cards), up from $35.6B in 2015 and $23.8B in 2014.
- Growth strategy: Efficient seller acquisition with strong cross-sell/up-sell opportunities; growing presence among larger sellers (annualized GPV > $125,000), which accounted for 42% of GPV in Q4 2016, up from 39% in Q4 2015.

structure.title: Business
structure.heading: Item 1. Business
structure.start_phrase: We started Square in February 2009 to enable businesses (sellers) to accept card payments, an important capability that was previously inaccessible tomany businesses.
structure.summary:
- Company overview and mission: Square (founded 2009) aims to economically empower sellers with an integrated, accessible commerce ecosystem to start, run, and grow their businesses.
- Cohesive ecosystem: Full-service managed payments as the foundation; fast onboarding; in-person (swipe, dip, tap) and online (Invoices, Virtual Terminal, e-commerce) acceptance; buyer-facing Square Cash for P2P and business payments.
- Hardware: Free magstripe reader; contactless and chip reader; chip card reader; Square Stand with peripheral support.
- Point-of-sale software and services: Square Point of Sale with Dashboard analytics; employee/location management, timecards, Payroll; customer engagement (feedback, marketing, loyalty); vertical solutions (Appointments, Invoices, Inventory); new Square for Retail with advanced inventory, PO, COGS, barcode scanning, clienteling.
- Developer platform: “Build with Square” APIs (POS, e-commerce, items/inventory, reporting/analytics, employee management) and App Marketplace integrations (e.g., QuickBooks, BigCommerce).
- Square Capital: Loan facilitation via partner bank using real-time payment/POS data; automated repayments as a % of card sales; majority funding via forward-flow sales to institutional investors; since May 2014, 200,000+ loans/MCAs totaling $1.3B.
- Caviar: Restaurant delivery marketplace expanding seller reach; fees to consumers (delivery/service) and restaurants (seller fee); active in multiple U.S. markets.
- Monetization: Transaction fees (transparent, covering reporting, next-day or instant settlement, receipts, dispute management, PCI); plus subscriptions and service fees for advanced features; transaction-based revenue as % of GPV was 2.93% (2016), 2.95% (2015), 2.98% (2014); instant deposit available for an extra fee.
- Scale and financials: 2016 GPV $49.7B (vs. $35.6B in 2015, $23.8B in 2014); about 1B card payments from ~245M cards in 2016; 2016 total net revenue $1.709B (up 35% YoY), adjusted revenue $686.6M (up 52% YoY); 2016 net loss $(171.6)M; adjusted EBITDA $44.9M; larger sellers (> $125k annualized GPV) were 42% of Q4’16 GPV; diversified seller base across industries and geographies (U.S., Canada, Japan, Australia); no customer >10% of GPV or net revenue in 2016.
- Seller base and growth: Efficient seller acquisition, cross-sell/upsell opportunities, growing penetration of larger sellers.
- Sales and marketing: Strong brand with NPS ~70; multi-channel direct marketing; retail distribution in 36,000+ stores (e.g., Apple, Amazon, Best Buy, Staples, Target, Walgreens); direct sales for larger sellers; partnerships and developer ecosystem; ongoing in-product communications and communities.
- Technology and product development: Mobile-first, platform-agnostic; tightly integrated hardware/software/payments; biweekly software releases; scalable platform with heavy use of data science and machine learning (automated risk assessment for >99.95% of transactions); in-house hardware design, third-party manufacturing; 2016 product development expense $268.5M.
- Transaction processing model: Roles and flow across PSP (Square), acquiring processors/banks, card networks, and issuing banks; fee components include processor fees, network assessments (<0.15% typically), and interchange (averaging 1.5%–2.0% plus fixed per transaction, varying by card/transaction); settlement timelines (next-day ACH or same-day instant deposit), ACH fees minimal; Square is merchant of record.
- Competition: Traditional acquirers/payment processors (often costly, long-term contracts); point solutions in POS/analytics/inventory/marketing; alternative lenders; delivery services; P2P providers. Square differentiates on an integrated, cohesive, self-serve, dependable ecosystem.
- Intellectual property: Mixed protections (patents, trademarks, copyrights, trade secrets, contracts); as of Dec 31, 2016, 229 issued patents and 588 applications globally (expiring 2022–2035); active trademark/domain strategy; uses some third-party and open-source technology.
- Regulation and compliance: U.S. money transmission licensing and FinCEN MSB registration; localized international services (Canada, Japan, Australia) with local oversight (e.g., AUSTRAC); consumer financial protection (CFPB and others); AML program and sanctions compliance; privacy/data protection; communications regulations for emails/SMS; other evolving areas (product liability, import/export, accessibility, insurance, marketing, labor/tax for Payroll expansion).
- Employees and corporate info: 1,853 full-time employees as of Dec 31, 2016; non-unionized; HQ in San Francisco; incorporated in Delaware (2009); investor relations and SEC filing access info; use of website/Twitter for disclosures.
- Early risk factors: Dependence on a strong, trusted brand; potential slowdown in growth tied to seller retention/acquisition and product adoption; ongoing net losses with continued investment may delay or prevent profitability.

structure.heading: Item 1A. Risk Factors
structure.start_phrase:
Investing

structure.summary:
- Section: Item 1A. Risk Factors from an Annual Report on Form 10-K, warning that investing involves a high degree of risk and the listed risks are not exhaustive; adverse outcomes could materially affect the business and stock price.
- Brand risk: The business relies on a strong, trusted brand built on seller and buyer trust, technology leadership, and high-quality, secure services. Negative publicity, product/service quality issues, risk management failures, privacy/security incidents, regulatory actions, litigation, complaint handling, and misconduct by employees or partners could damage reputation and reduce product use.
- Growth sustainability: Past revenue growth (2014–2016) is not guaranteed; the growth rate is expected to decline and could do so faster than anticipated.
- Customer retention and acquisition: Sellers are not bound by long-term contracts and can switch with relatively low cost; activity may fall due to satisfaction levels, support effectiveness, pricing, competitive offerings, macroeconomic conditions, or lower end-customer spending.
- Expansion within accounts: Growth depends on existing sellers broadening usage, attracting new sellers (including larger ones), and successfully launching new products/services.
- Product innovation risk: Continued investment in offerings (e.g., Square Cash, Caviar, Instant Deposit, Invoices) may not yield success, which could slow or reduce growth.
- Profitability risk: The company has a history of net losses and a significant accumulated deficit and plans to continue substantial investments (personnel, sales/marketing, direct marketing, referral programs, free/subsidized hardware/services, product development, office/infrastructure, and international expansion), which may prevent achieving or maintaining profitability.

nodes.summary:
- Rising operating costs: increasing expenses for acquiring and supporting new/larger sellers, public-company compliance, and advertising; upfront seller onboarding costs versus later revenue recognition may prolong losses if revenue growth and expense control lag.
- Long-term trade-offs: strategic choices made to improve seller and user experience may depress short-term results, conflict with investor expectations, and may not deliver anticipated long-term benefits.
- Data security and privacy risks: extensive collection and processing of sensitive data (PII, PCI data, bank details, seller performance data, PHI) across the company, sellers, partners, and third-party data centers; HIPAA obligations; potential breaches via malware, phishing, hacking, or errors could damage reputation, trigger regulatory scrutiny, penalties, remediation costs, and liability (including card reissuance costs); exposure also if company confidential information is disclosed.
- Platform security dependence: the reliability and security of the payments platform are critical; real or perceived breaches could cause seller loss, hinder new seller acquisition, drive significant remediation spend, and lead to legal and regulatory actions; third-party provider breaches pose similar risks.
- Risk management limitations: responsibility to vet and monitor customers and transactions; exposure to fraud, money laundering, and terrorist financing; inherent security–convenience trade-offs; growing exposure with larger sellers and new markets/products; potential inaccuracies in forecasting losses; ineffective policies or errors could result in major financial losses and civil/criminal liability.
- Chargebacks and refunds exposure: liability when disputes resolve against sellers or when sellers cannot reimburse (e.g., insolvency); EMV liability shift increases seller responsibility and reimbursement needs; not all readers are EMV-compliant; absence of seller reserves and occasional waivers increase risk; excessive chargebacks could lead to network fines, higher fees, or loss of card acceptance.
- Revenue concentration and diversification risk: heavy reliance on managed payments transaction fees; efforts to expand products/services and markets may fail, slow growth, introduce operational/technical challenges, service disruptions, and may not recoup investments, harming reputation and business.
- Need for continuous innovation: success depends on delivering enhancements and new features amid rapid changes in payments/POS, financial and marketing services; evolving technologies include e-commerce, mobile commerce, contactless/NFC, cryptocurrencies, and tokenization; failure to keep pace could materially and adversely affect the business.

- New products and market expansions may face acceptance, technical, and operational challenges; service disruptions could damage reputation, limit growth, and delay or prevent investment payback.

nodes.summary: The excerpt outlines significant operational, financial, and regulatory risks. It emphasizes vulnerability to service interruptions from cyberattacks, human error, and natural disasters (notably in the seismically active San Francisco Bay Area), noting limited redundancy, potentially inadequate disaster recovery, insufficient insurance, and increasing regulatory scrutiny of business continuity that could divert resources. It warns that outages and performance degradation can lead to revenue loss, high remediation costs, reputational damage, customer attrition, and potential claims. It details specific risks to Square Capital, including reliance on third-party investors to purchase bank-originated loans, sensitivity to pricing and servicing fees, exposure to adverse macroeconomic conditions that can increase defaults and reduce seller eligibility, limited recourse on seller breaches, and dependence on a bank partner amid regulatory and litigation scrutiny of partnered lending; losing or changing that partnership could necessitate costly alternatives or a reversion to MCAs. The text also highlights plans to explore new credit models that may require additional licenses, partnerships, or capabilities, with the risk that evolving regulations could hinder growth. More broadly, the company is subject to extensive, changing domestic and international laws across consumer protection, privacy/data protection, fair lending, financial services, labor, and marketing, with potential for audits, investigations, fines, and burdensome compliance. It underscores growing obligations around collection, use, security, and transfer of personal data, the costs of compliance with privacy/security standards, and the business impact of any real or perceived noncompliance. structure.title: Management’s Discussion and Analysis of Financial Condition and Results of Operations
structure.heading: Item 7. Management’s Discussion and Analysis of Financial Condition and Results of Operations
structure.start_phrase: You should read the following discussion and analysis in conjunction with the information set forth under “Selected Financial Data” and our consolidatedfinancial statements and related notes included elsewhere in this Annual Report on Form 10-K.
structure.summary:
- Scope and forward-looking statements: Management’s Discussion and Analysis (MD&A) outlining performance, liquidity, capital resources, risks, and uncertainties, to be read with the financial statements and Selected Financial Data.
- Business overview: Square’s commerce ecosystem combining managed payments, POS software, analytics, and hardware; ability to accept in-person (magstripe, EMV, NFC) and online payments; consumer offering via Square Cash. Monetization primarily through per-transaction fees, plus subscriptions and services.
- Ecosystem components and monetization:
  - Managed payments: reporting/analytics, next-day settlement, digital receipts, dispute/chargeback management, PCI compliance; revenue recognized net of refunds at authorization.
  - Software and services: Employee Management, Customer Engagement, Payroll, Appointments, Instant Deposit, Gift Cards, and Marketplace; monetized via subscription, service, or transaction fees.
  - Square Capital: transition in 2016 from merchant cash advances (MCAs) to bank-originated loans purchased by Square and largely sold to third-party investors; revenue from loan sale gains and ongoing servicing, plus recognition on retained loans held for sale; mitigates balance sheet risk.
  - Caviar: food ordering/delivery service; revenue from restaurant fees, delivery, and consumer service fees, recognized upon delivery net of refunds.
  - Hardware: contactless & chip readers, chip card readers, Square Stand, third-party peripherals; revenue recognized upon delivery; certain hardware (Stand; contactless & chip reader) priced below cost for strategic reasons.
- Geographic footprint: sellers across the U.S., Canada, Japan, and Australia; broad industry mix from small vendors to multi-location businesses.
- Key operating metrics and performance (2014–2016):
  - GPV grew from $23.8B (2014) to $35.6B (2015) to $49.7B (2016).
  - Total net revenue rose from $850.2M (2014) to $1.27B (2015) to $1.71B (2016).
  - Adjusted Revenue increased from $276.3M (2014) to $452.2M (2015) to $686.6M (2016).
  - Net loss attributable to common stockholders narrowed to $(171.6)M in 2016 from $(212.0)M in 2015; Adjusted EBITDA turned positive in 2016.
- Revenue and cost presentation updates: renaming of line items to transaction-based revenue/costs (including Starbucks), and subscription and services-based revenue/costs to better reflect monetization; underlying components unchanged.
- Detailed revenue drivers:
  - Transaction-based revenue up 39% in 2016 on 39% GPV growth; continued positive dollar-based retention and new seller additions.
  - Starbucks transaction-based revenue declined 45% in 2016 and ceased after Starbucks’ full transition to another processor by Q4 2016.
  - Subscription and services-based revenue up 123% in 2016 (to 8% of total), driven by Square Capital and Caviar, with contributions from newer services like Instant Deposit.
  - Hardware revenue up 171% in 2016, led by contactless & chip reader shipments post-2015 launch.
- Cost of revenue and margins:
  - Transaction-based costs tracked GPV growth; Starbucks costs fell faster than Starbucks revenue in 2016 due to higher processing rates paid by Starbucks from Oct 2015.
  - Subscription/services costs increased with Caviar scale and amortization of developed products.
  - Hardware costs up with volumes, but improved mix (contactless & chip reader versus Stand) benefited margins.
  - Amortization of acquired technology increased due to prior acquisitions.
- Operating expenses and notable items:
  - Product development is the largest expense; increased with engineering/product/design hiring and higher share-based compensation (SBC).
  - Sales and marketing rose with headcount, Square Cash P2P costs; paid marketing stable in 2016; expectation of S&M declining as a percentage of revenue long term.
  - General and administrative increased significantly in 2016 due to scaling support functions, first-year public company costs, higher third-party services, and a non-recurring $48M litigation settlement related to Robert E. Morley (Q1 2016).
  - Transaction, loan, and advance losses decreased in 2016 despite GPV growth due to improved risk operations and data science; historical transaction losses ~0.1% of GPV (2014–2016). No loss exposure on loans sold to third parties; retained loans at lower of cost or fair value with fair value exceeding cost; MCA receivables still carried with allowances.
  - Amortization of acquired customer assets declined in 2016 as certain assets reached end of life.
- Interest and taxes:
  - Net interest/other swung to slight net income in 2016 due to interest on marketable securities and FX fluctuations.
  - Provision for income taxes decreased in 2016; 2015 increase tied to reduced tax benefits from acquisitions.
  - 2015 included a $32.2M deemed dividend on Series E preferred stock (non-recurring).
- Quarterly results and trends:
  - Eight-quarter tables include revenue/costs, expenses, SBC by function, and non-GAAP metrics (Adjusted Revenue, Adjusted EBITDA, Adjusted Net Income (Loss)) with reconciliations.
  - Seasonality: strongest transaction-based revenue in Q4, weakest in Q1 (holiday-driven GPV); subscription/services and hardware show less seasonality, with hardware tied to product launches/promotions.
  - G&A includes $50M litigation expense in Q1 2016, later settled.
- Liquidity and capital resources:
  - Year-end 2016: $452.0M cash and cash equivalents; $87.3M marketable securities; restricted cash of $36.7M; total cash, equivalents, and investments of $539.3M.
  - Cash flows (2016): operating +$23.1M; investing $(122.7)M (marketable securities purchases, capex); financing +$90.7M (equity proceeds from option/warrant/ESPP exercises).
  - IPO in Nov 2015 provided $245.7M net proceeds; historical funding through preferred stock pre-IPO.
  - Undrawn $375.0M revolving secured credit facility maturing Nov 2020; variable interest terms; customary fees.
  - Transition from MCAs to bank-originated loans (purchased and largely sold to investors) completed in Q1 2016; small retained loan balances.
  - Management believes liquidity is sufficient for at least 12 months; may pursue additional financing as needed.
  - Restricted cash supports letters of credit for processing and lease collateral; working capital fluctuates daily with GPV and period-end timing.
- Contractual obligations and commitments:
  - Operating leases through 2025; capital leases; purchase commitments to hardware suppliers; schedule of payments presented.
  - No off-balance sheet arrangements.
- Critical accounting policies and estimates: revenue recognition; accrued transaction losses; valuation of loans held for sale; business combinations; goodwill and intangible assets; income taxes; share-based compensation. Emphasis on estimates and judgment under GAAP.
- Market risk disclosures (Item 7A):
  - Interest rate sensitivity: limited impact due to short-duration investments; ability to hold to maturity; potential floating-rate exposure if drawing on credit facility.
  - Foreign currency risk: most revenue in USD; operating exposure in JPY, CAD, AUD; FX fluctuations can affect results.

- Accounting for loans held for sale: initially designated as HFS, with potential reclassification to held for investment if intent changes (no reclassifications to date); carried at the lower of cost or fair value; fair value estimated using industry-standard models (e.g., discounted cash flows); gains/losses realized upon sale.
- Settlements receivable: amounts due from third-party payment processors, typically collected within 1–2 business days; no valuation allowance due to strong counterparties and no historical collection issues.
- Provision for uncollectible receivables related to merchant cash advances (MCAs): merchant cash advance receivables presented net of an allowance; allowance based on historical experience, current merchant processing volume, and other relevant factors; additions recognized in transaction and advance losses; charge-offs reduce the allowance; company transitioned from MCAs to loans in Q1 2016, with subsequent activity limited to updates/write-offs/recoveries; no loss exposure on MCAs sold to third-party investors under existing arrangements.
- Customer funds: balances stored by customers in the Square Cash App or in transit are held as short-term bank deposits; a corresponding customer funds obligation is recorded as a liability.
- Inventory: includes contactless and chip readers, chip card readers, Square Stand, and third-party peripherals; valued at lower of cost (FIFO) or market; write-downs recorded for obsolete or excess items based on expected demand and market conditions.
- Deferred magstripe reader costs: costs (including packaging and shipping) capitalized in other current assets while on hand; expensed as marketing when shipped to distributors or end customers.
- Property and equipment: recorded at cost and depreciated straight-line over estimated useful lives—capitalized software (18 months), computer and data center equipment (3 years), furniture and fixtures (7 years), and leasehold improvements (lesser of useful life or remaining lease term).

nodes.summary:

- States inventory accounting for hardware (readers, Square Stand, peripherals) at lower of cost (FIFO) or market, with write-downs for obsolescence or excess.

- Provides property and equipment policies: recorded at cost less straight-line depreciation; useful lives include capitalized software (18 months), computer and data center equipment (3 years), furniture and fixtures (7 years), and leasehold improvements (lesser of useful life or lease term); gains/losses on disposals recognized in operating expenses.
- Describes capitalization of internal-use software development costs once criteria are met, amortized to product development or allocated to subscription/service costs; discloses amounts capitalized and amortized for 2014–2016.
- Summarizes lease accounting for office space and equipment under capital and operating leases with straight-line rent recognition; treatment of landlord allowances; cash flow classification for leasehold improvement spend and reimbursements; recognition of asset retirement obligations with disclosed balances as of December 31, 2016.
- Explains business combinations: purchase price allocation to identifiable assets and liabilities at fair value, with excess as goodwill; measurement period adjustments recorded against goodwill, and post-measurement changes recognized in earnings.
- Sets out impairment policies for long-lived assets and finite-lived intangibles using undiscounted cash flow recoverability tests and fair value measures (DCF, market values, appraisals); notes no impairments recorded in the periods presented.
- Details goodwill accounting and annual impairment testing (as of December 31), including the option for a qualitative assessment to determine if quantitative testing is necessary.

nodes.title: Capitalized Software

Cash flows: improvements in investing; landlord reimbursements in operating.
- Asset retirement obligations (AROs): Record fair value liability with offsetting asset based on assumptions about legal obligations, settlement timing/amounts, discount and inflation rates; accrete liability and depreciate asset. At December 31, 2016: ARO liability $3.2M (gross of accretion); associated asset $2.6M (net of depreciation).
- Business combinations: Allocate purchase price to identifiable assets and liabilities at fair value; excess recorded as goodwill. Measurement period up to one year for adjustments to fair values with offsets to goodwill; post-measurement adjustments recorded in the income statement.
- Long-lived assets (including finite-lived intangibles): Test for impairment when indicators exist; compare carrying amount to undiscounted cash flows; if not recoverable, write down to fair value determined via valuation techniques (DCF, market, appraisals). No impairment charges recorded in the periods presented.
- Goodwill: Test annually on December 31 and upon triggering events; recognize impairment if carrying amount exceeds reporting unit fair value; option to perform a qualitative assessment to determine if a quantitative test is needed.

- Business combinations: purchase price allocation to identifiable assets and liabilities at fair value, recognition of goodwill for excess consideration, measurement period (up to one year) for adjustments recorded to goodwill, and post-measurement adjustments flowing through the income statement.
- Impairment of long-lived assets and intangibles: trigger-based recoverability tests using undiscounted cash flows and recognition of impairment to fair value if not recoverable; valuation methods include DCF, market quotes, and appraisals; no impairments recorded in the periods presented.
- Goodwill: annual impairment testing on December 31 (and interim if indicators arise), recognition of loss if carrying amount exceeds fair value, and option to perform a qualitative assessment before a quantitative test.

Cash payments for improvements are investing cash flows; landlord reimbursements are operating cash flows.
- Asset retirement obligations (AROs): Recognized at estimated fair value with offsetting asset based on assumptions (legal obligation, timing, amounts, discount/inflation). Liability accreted and asset depreciated. As of Dec 31, 2016: ARO liability $3.2m (gross of accretion); associated asset $2.6m (net of depreciation).
- Business combinations: Purchase price allocated to identifiable assets and liabilities at fair value; excess is goodwill. Adjustments during the measurement period (up to one year) offset goodwill; afterward, adjustments flow through the income statement.
- Long-lived assets and finite-lived intangibles: Tested for recoverability when indicators arise using undiscounted cash flows; impairments measured to fair value (DCF, market data, third-party appraisals). No impairment charges recorded for the periods presented.
- Goodwill: Tested annually on December 31 and more frequently if needed; impairment recognized if carrying amount exceeds reporting unit fair value. Option to perform a qualitative assessment to determine if a quantitative test is necessary.

nodes.title: Long-Lived Assets, including Goodwill and Acquired Intangibles
nodes.heading: 7.1.26 Long-Lived Assets, including Goodwill and Acquired Intangibles
nodes.start_phrase: The Company evaluates the recoverability of property and equipment and finite lived intangible assets for impairment whenever events or circumstances indicate that the carrying amounts of such assets may not be recoverable.
nodes.summary:
- Asset disposals: When assets are retired or disposed, their cost and accumulated depreciation are removed from the accounts, and any gain or loss is recorded in operating expenses.
- Capitalized internal-use software: Costs are capitalized once criteria are met; prior costs are expensed. Capitalized amounts are recorded in property and equipment and amortized straight-line over the software’s useful life, recognized in product development or allocated to subscription/service costs. Disclosures include amounts capitalized and amortized for 2014–2016.
- Leases: The company has non-cancellable capital and operating leases; rent is recognized on a straight-line basis. Leasehold improvements are capitalized and depreciated over the lesser of lease term or asset life; landlord allowances reduce rent expense straight-line. Cash payments for improvements are investing cash flows; landlord reimbursements are operating cash flows.
- Asset retirement obligations (AROs): The company records ARO liabilities at estimated fair value with an offsetting asset, using assumptions about legal obligations, timing, amounts, discount, and inflation rates; liabilities are accreted and assets depreciated. ARO balances at December 31, 2016 are disclosed.
- Business combinations: Purchase price is allocated to identifiable assets and liabilities at fair value; excess is goodwill. Adjustments within the measurement period (up to one year) adjust goodwill; afterward, changes flow through the income statement.
- Long-lived assets impairment: Property, equipment, and finite-lived intangibles are tested for recoverability upon indicators of impairment using undiscounted cash flows; impairments reflect excess of carrying value over fair value determined via valuation techniques. No impairments recorded in the periods presented.
- Goodwill impairment: Tested annually (December 31) or upon triggering events, with an optional qualitative assessment to determine if a quantitative test is needed. No goodwill impairments recorded in the periods presented.
- Acquired intangibles: Include acquired technology and customer relationships. Technology is amortized in cost of revenue; customer relationships are amortized in operating expenses. Useful lives are reassessed periodically.
- Customers payable: Liability for amounts owed to sellers net of the company’s earned revenue, including timing differences (typically settled within one business day), risk management holds, and amounts for customers without linked bank accounts.
- Accrued transaction losses: Reserve for expected chargebacks and fraud, estimated using current data, expected future chargebacks, and historical loss trends. Additions impact current operations; realized losses are charged against the reserve and presented within transaction and advance losses.
- Recent accounting pronouncements:
  - ASC 606 Revenue: Effective for fiscal years beginning after Dec 15, 2017; the company will adopt using the modified retrospective approach, not early adopting, and is assessing financial statement and systems impacts.
  - ASU 2015-11 Inventory: Measures inventory at lower of cost and net realizable value, effective for fiscal years beginning after Dec 15, 2016; impact under evaluation.
  - ASU 2015-17 Deferred taxes: Requires classification of all deferred tax assets and liabilities as noncurrent, effective for fiscal years beginning after Dec 15, 2016.

- Customers payable: Represents amounts owed to sellers net of the company’s earned revenue, including timing-related amounts typically settled within one business day, holds under risk management policies, and funds held for customers without a linked bank account.
- Accrued transaction losses: A reserve for expected chargebacks and fraud is estimated using current data, expectations of future chargebacks, and historical loss trends; additions impact current results and recognized losses reduce the reserve. These are presented in transaction and advance losses on the income statement.

Effective for fiscal years after Dec 15, 2017; the company will not early adopt and plans modified retrospective adoption, assessing financial statement and system impacts.

nodes.title: Accrued Transaction Losses
nodes.heading: 7.1.28 Accrued Transaction Losses

nodes.summary:

Acquired technology is amortized straight-line within cost of revenue; customer relationships are amortized straight-line within operating expenses. The Company reassesses useful lives regularly for potential revisions.
- Customers payable: Liability for amounts owed to sellers net of revenue earned, including timing differences due to next-day settlement, funds held per risk management policies, and amounts held for customers without linked bank accounts.
- Accrued transaction losses: Reserve for chargebacks and fraudulent transactions based on available data, expected future chargebacks, and historical loss rates. Additions recorded in current operations; charges made when losses are recognized. Classified within transaction and advance losses on the income statement.
- Recent accounting pronouncements:
  - ASU 2014-09 (Revenue from Contracts with Customers) and related updates: Core principle of recognizing revenue upon transfer of goods/services for expected consideration. Effective for fiscal years after Dec 15, 2017. Company will not early adopt, plans modified retrospective adoption, and is assessing financial statement impact and system changes.

  - ASU 2015-17 (Balance Sheet Classification of Deferred Taxes): Classify all deferred tax assets and liabilities as noncurrent. Effective for fiscal years after Dec 15, 2016.
